title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.1 What this book will teach you
This book is about answering questions with data that have a location attached. Where are thefts and burglaries concentrated in a town? Which neighborhoods are far from a hospital? How much forest was lost in the mountains after a hurricane? Questions like these come up in planning, public health, business, environmental science, and nearly every other field, and they share a common set of skills: finding the right data, turning it into useful information, and communicating what you found.
This first chapter steps back from the code to look at the big picture. It explains what spatial data science is, why location deserves special attention, and what kinds of questions you will be able to answer by the end of the book. Every later chapter fills in one part of that picture.
By the end of the book, you will be able to do three things:
Each of these builds on the one before it. You can’t make a useful map until you can load and clean the data behind it, and you can’t answer a question until you can turn raw data into something that speaks to it.

title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.2 What is spatial data science?

1.2.1 From data to wisdom
It helps to start with the word data itself, and with how it differs from the things we actually want from it. A common way to describe this is a ladder with four rungs (Figure 1.1).

Data are facts and figures: a column of numbers, a list of addresses, the pixel values of a satellite image.
Information is data organized so that it is useful: a table of average income by county, or a map of where those addresses fall.
Knowledge is information accumulated and integrated over time and across a broad range of situations: an understanding of why income varies the way it does, built from many studies of many places.
Wisdom is the application of principles, reason, and knowledge to discern what is true and right: deciding what a city should actually do about it.








flowchart LR
  A["Data<br/>facts and figures"] --> B["Information<br/>organized and useful"]
  B --> C["Knowledge<br/>integrated over time<br/>and situations"]
  C --> D["Wisdom<br/>judging what is<br/>true and right"]




Figure 1.1: The data–information–knowledge–wisdom ladder. Each step adds organization, context, and judgment. This book focuses on the first step: turning data into information.





Most of this book is about the first step, from data to information. That step is where code does the most work: no one can read a million rows of data, but anyone can read a well-made map or a short table that summarizes them. The later steps depend on people, but they can only be as good as the information they rest on.


1.2.2 Spatial, data, science
The name of the field is a good summary of what it involves. Each of its three words covers a different set of skills (Table 1.1).



Table 1.1: The three parts of spatial data science, and some of what each involves.

Spatial is about what we study: things that happen in places, measured by sources such as satellites, environmental sensors, the Census, and transportation networks. Data is about how we handle it: reading files in many formats, organizing and cleaning them, storing them, and visualizing them. Science is about why: asking a clear question, structuring an analysis to answer it, reporting the results, and critiquing them honestly, including your own.

title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.3 Why does location matter?
Everything happens somewhere. From changes in trade policy to the spread of a disease, location is a fundamental attribute of almost everything we might want to study. Knowing where something happens often tells you a great deal about why it happens, and about who it affects. A few examples show how widely this applies:

Urban planning. Where should a city build new parks or schools so that the most people can reach them?
Environmental science. How does air or water pollution spread across a region from its sources?
Public health. Where are the hotspots of a disease outbreak, and what do those places have in common?
Business. Where should a company put its next store or warehouse, and how should goods move between them?
Social sciences. How are demographic trends, such as aging or migration, distributed across a country?

In each case, a table without locations would miss the point. The question is about place.






TipThink about it



How could you use spatial data science to understand the effects of a change in tariffs, the taxes a country charges on imported goods? What would you map? Which places might be affected most: ports, farming regions that export crops, towns built around one factory? What data would you need to find out?

title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.4 The spatial data science workflow
Whatever the question, a spatial data science project moves through the same three stages (Figure 1.2).







flowchart LR
  Q["Question"] --> A["Get reliable data"]
  A --> B["Understand and<br/>process the data"]
  B --> C["Find patterns and<br/>communicate results"]
  C -.-> Q




Figure 1.2: The spatial data science workflow. A question leads to data, data must be processed before they can be analyzed, and results must be communicated. What you learn often raises a new question.






Get reliable data. Whatever question you want to ask, the answer can only be as good as the data behind it. That means knowing where your data came from, who collected it and how, what each column means, and what is missing.
Understand and process the data. Real data are rarely ready to use. They need to be read into R, cleaned, reshaped, joined to other data, and often given a location or put into the right coordinate system. This stage usually takes the most time.
Find patterns and communicate the results. Look for patterns, relationships, and trends in the data, then present them in a way that answers your question. A clear map, table, or paragraph is the product of the whole project. Results that no one can understand might as well not exist.

The arrow back to the start of Figure 1.2 matters, too. Answering one question usually raises another, and good projects often loop through the workflow several times.

title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.5 Spatial thinking
Much of traditional statistics, and much of data science, treats each observation as independent of the others: knowing one tells you nothing about the next. For data about places, that assumption is usually wrong. Spatial thinking means taking seriously how location connects observations. Three ideas come up again and again in this book.

1.5.1 Spatial autocorrelation
Spatial autocorrelation is the tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than things that are far apart. Neighboring homes tend to have similar values. Neighboring counties tend to have similar incomes, voting patterns, and rainfall. The geographer Waldo Tobler put it as what is now called the first law of geography: “everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things” (Tobler 1970).
Spatial autocorrelation is both a problem and an opportunity. It is a problem because standard statistical tests assume independence, and they can be badly overconfident when observations are really echoes of their neighbors. It is an opportunity because it is often exactly what we want to find: a cluster of high values is a hotspot, and hotspots are where to look first. Later chapters show how to measure it.


1.5.2 Scale
Scale is the level of detail you work at: individual addresses, neighborhoods, counties, states. A pattern that is clear at one scale can vanish, or even reverse, at another. A county can have a high average income while containing neighborhoods with very low incomes, and a trend across a whole city might not exist within any single neighborhood.
The way areas are drawn matters as well as their size. Grouping the same individual data into different sets of boundaries, such as different districts of the same size, can change the results of an analysis. This is known as the modifiable areal unit problem (Openshaw 1984). The practical lesson is to choose your scale deliberately, to match the question, and to be careful about drawing conclusions at one scale from data collected at another.


1.5.3 Spatial heterogeneity
Spatial heterogeneity means that relationships between variables can change from place to place. The link between, say, distance to downtown and home prices might be strong in one city and weak in another, or even differ between the east and west sides of the same city. A single number that summarizes a relationship for a whole region can hide those differences. Spatial data science often means asking not just “what is the relationship?” but “where is it strongest, and where does it break down?”






NoteThree questions to ask of any spatial data




Are nearby values similar? (spatial autocorrelation)
Would the pattern look different with larger or smaller areas? (scale)
Does the relationship I’m studying hold everywhere, or only in some places? (spatial heterogeneity)

A spatial data science question is one where location is part of the answer, and where data can settle it. Here are some examples from North Carolina. Notice the key word in each, which hints at the kind of analysis it needs.

title: 1  What is Spatial Data Science?
text:
1.10 Summary

Spatial data science uses data with locations to answer questions about the world. It combines the spatial (what we study), data skills (how we handle it), and science (how we ask and answer questions).
Data become information when they are organized to be useful. Information, accumulated and integrated, becomes knowledge, and knowledge applied with judgment becomes wisdom. This book focuses on turning data into information.
Everything happens somewhere, and location matters in planning, environmental science, public health, business, the social sciences, and beyond.
A project moves from a question to reliable data, to processing, to finding and communicating results, and often loops back to a new question.
Spatial data are rarely independent. Watch for spatial autocorrelation (near things are alike), scale (patterns change with the size and shape of areas), and spatial heterogeneity (relationships change from place to place).
Our tools are R and RStudio, with the tidyverse, sf, and tmap packages.

title: 2  R, RStudio, and R Markdown
text:
2.1 What is R?
Every chapter after this one asks you to do spatial data science: download data, clean it, analyze it, and map it. You will do all of that by writing code. This chapter introduces the three tools you will use for every lab and assignment, and the small vocabulary you need to read and write your first lines of R.
The three tools are easy to mix up, so it helps to keep one sentence in mind from the start: R is the language, RStudio is the workspace, and R Markdown is the document format. The first half of the chapter takes each in turn. The second half covers the building blocks of code that appear in every script you will write.
R is a programming language and free software environment for statistical computing and graphics. It was created by statisticians, and its strengths still reflect that: cleaning, analyzing, modeling, and visualizing data. Statisticians, data scientists, and geographers all use it for the same reason. A few lines of R can do what would take dozens of clicks in a spreadsheet or a desktop GIS, and those lines can be run again tomorrow.
On its own, R knows how to do arithmetic, statistics, and basic plots. What makes it useful for geography is its packages (also called libraries): bundles of code, written by other users, that add new abilities. There are thousands of them. In this course you will use sf for vector data such as points, lines, and polygons, terra for rasters, tidyverse for cleaning and reshaping data, and tmap and ggplot2 for maps.

title: 2  R, RStudio, and R Markdown
text:
2.1.1 Why use R?
R has four strengths that make it the tool for this course.

Power. R has a huge range of tools for statistics, machine learning, and spatial analysis, and new methods often appear as R packages before they appear anywhere else.
Visualization. R makes high-quality, fully customizable plots, charts, and maps. Every figure in this book was made in R.
Reproducibility. A script records every step of an analysis, so you, a classmate, or a reviewer can rerun it and check the result.
Community. A large, global community of users builds packages, answers questions, and writes tutorials. When you get stuck, someone has almost always asked the same question online.

Reproducibility matters most for us. A point-and-click GIS workflow is hard to repeat exactly: which tool did you run, with which settings, in which order? An R script answers all of those questions in writing. When the data are updated, or when you find a mistake in step two of ten, you fix it and run the script again, and every later step updates with it.
There are practical reasons, too. R is free and open source, so everything you learn here keeps working after you graduate, with no license fees. It is updated frequently, it is popular in both research and industry, and it is consistently ranked among the most widely used languages for statistics and data analysis. The skills transfer to jobs and to graduate research.

title: 2  R, RStudio, and R Markdown
text:
2.2 What is RStudio?
You can type R commands into a plain window, but almost nobody works that way. RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R: one window where you write code, run it, see the results, and check your data. A good way to think about the relationship is that R is the engine and RStudio is the dashboard. R does the computing underneath; RStudio is where you work.
Because RStudio drives R, you need both, and you must install R first, then RStudio. RStudio cannot run any code until R is installed. Both are free. Installation steps are in Section 2.6 at the end of this chapter.

2.2.1 The four panes
When you open RStudio, the window is divided into four panes (Figure 2.1).






Figure 2.1: RStudio’s default four-pane layout, just after opening. The Editor is at the top left, the Console at the bottom left, the Environment at the top right, and Files, Plots, and Help at the bottom right.






Table 2.1: The four panes of RStudio.










Pane
Default position
What it is for




Editor
Top left
Writing and saving scripts and R Markdown files


Console
Bottom left
Running commands and reading results, warnings, and errors


Environment
Top right
Listing the variables and data currently in memory


Files, Plots, Help
Bottom right
Browsing folders, viewing graphs, and reading documentation






The difference between the Editor and the Console is the most important one in Table 2.1. The Editor is where your work is saved. Anything you type there can be kept in a file and run again. The Console is for quick tests: R runs a command the moment you press Enter, but nothing you type there is saved. A useful habit is to experiment in the Console and keep what works in the Editor.
The Environment pane lists every variable you have created, with a short description of what it holds. It is the first place to look when you are debugging: if a variable you expected is missing, or holds something unexpected, the Environment will show it. The bottom-right pane holds several tabs, including Files, Plots, Packages, and Help.


2.2.2 RStudio during a working session
Figure 2.2 shows RStudio partway through an analysis, with every pane in use.






Figure 2.2: RStudio during a working session. Code in the Editor (top left) has been run, the variables it created are listed in the Environment (top right), output and an error message appear in the Console (bottom left), and the resulting scatterplot is in the Plots pane (bottom right).



The screenshot captures the loop you will repeat constantly:

Write a line of code in the Editor.
Run it. Click Run, or press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Return on a Mac), to send the current line to the Console.
Check the Environment. If the line created a variable, it appears there.
Read the Console. Output, warnings, and errors print here.
Look at the Plots pane if the line drew a graph.

Notice the red error message in the Console of Figure 2.2. Errors are a normal part of writing code, and they are not something to skip past. Read them. They usually say what went wrong, and often where. (This one, “figure margins too large,” just means the Plots pane was too small to draw the graph, and it went away when the pane was enlarged.)

2.3 R scripts and R Markdown
There are two kinds of files you will write R in, and it is worth being clear about the difference (Table 2.2).



Table 2.2: R scripts compared with R Markdown documents.











R script
R Markdown




File extension
.R
.Rmd


Contains
Code only
Formatted text with code chunks


Notes and explanation
Comments that start with #
Ordinary text, headings, and lists


Produces
Results in the Console and Plots pane
A finished document in HTML, PDF, or Word


Best for
Short tasks and reusable code

An R script is only code. Anything in it that is not code has to be written as a comment. An R Markdown file mixes formatted text and code, so the explanation of an analysis lives right next to the analysis itself. It is easier to read and easier to share. All assignments in this course are R Markdown files, so you will write both kinds of content: prose in Markdown and code inside chunks.

2.3.1 What is R Markdown?
R Markdown is a file format for dynamic, reproducible documents. An .Rmd file combines text written in Markdown, a simple way of formatting plain text, with chunks of R code. When you knit the file, R runs every code chunk and places the results (numbers, tables, and plots) into a finished document, as HTML, PDF, or Word (Figure 2.3).







flowchart LR
  A["analysis.Rmd<br/>(text + code chunks)"] -- "Knit" --> B{{"R runs<br/>every chunk"}}
  B --> C["analysis.html<br/>(text + code + results)"]




Figure 2.3: Knitting an R Markdown file. R runs every code chunk from top to bottom and combines your text with the code’s results in a finished report.





The key idea is that the document and the analysis are the same file. If the data change, you knit again, and every number and figure in the report updates with them. Nothing has to be copied and pasted by hand, so nothing can fall out of date. In this course we mostly knit to HTML, because it is fastest and needs no extra software.






TipR Markdown and Quarto



This book is written in Quarto, the newer successor to R Markdown, made by the same developers. Quarto files end in .qmd instead of .Rmd, but the YAML header, Markdown text, and code chunks work the same way. Everything in this chapter applies to both.




2.3.2 Anatomy of an R Markdown file
Every R Markdown file has three kinds of content: a YAML header, Markdown text, and code chunks.
The YAML header sits at the very top of the file, between two lines of exactly three dashes. It holds metadata, which is data about data. Here it describes the document rather than the analysis: its title, author, date, and output format.
---
title: "My First R Markdown Document"
author: "Jane Doe"
date: "August 14, 2025"
output: html_document
---
R reads the header to know what to put at the top of the report and what kind of document to produce. YAML is picky: the dashes must be exactly three, each line needs a space after the colon, and indentation matters.
Markdown text is plain text with a few simple formatting marks. A line that starts with # becomes a heading (## a smaller heading, ### smaller still). Wrapping a word in single asterisks makes it italic, and double asterisks make it bold. A line that starts with - becomes an item in a bulleted list.
Code chunks hold R code. A chunk starts with three backticks followed by {r}, and ends with three backticks:
```{r}
1 + 2 + 3
```
The {r} tells R Markdown that the chunk contains R code. Click the small green “play” arrow at the top right of a chunk to run just that chunk. When the file is knit, the result prints directly below the chunk in the report:
1 + 2 + 3
#> [1] 6
The [1] in front of the answer is R’s way of saying “this is the first element of the result.” You will see it in front of almost every result R prints, and you can ignore it for now.
Putting the three pieces together, a complete (very short) R Markdown file looks like this:
---
title: "Lab 1"
author: "Jane Doe"
output: html_document
---

## How many months are in a century?

There are 12 months in a year and 100 years in a century.

```{r}
# Months in a century
months <- 12
years <- 100
months * years
```

So a century has **1,200** months.


2.3.3 The R Markdown workflow
You will follow the same four steps for every assignment.

Create a file. In RStudio, choose File > New File > R Markdown…, give the document a title, and click OK. RStudio opens a new file that already contains a YAML header and some example content.
Edit the document. Write your narrative in Markdown, and insert code chunks where you need them (Code > Insert Chunk, or Ctrl+Alt+I; Cmd+Option+I on a Mac).
Run code chunks as you go, by clicking each chunk’s green play arrow, to check that each one does what you expect.
Knit the document. Click Knit in the Editor toolbar. R builds an HTML report with all of your text, code, output, and plots, and opens it in a preview window.

Knitting does something important that is easy to miss: it reruns all of your code, from the top, in a fresh R session that knows nothing about what you have already run. A file that knits successfully is therefore a file that anyone can reproduce from scratch. If it fails to knit, the error message names the chunk that broke.


2.3.4 Keep all course files in one folder
Most of the errors students run into early in the semester are not really coding errors. They are file path errors: R cannot find a data file because the .Rmd file and the data are saved in different places. When you knit, R looks for files relative to the folder where the .Rmd file is saved, so a tidy folder structure prevents a whole category of “file not found” errors.
Create one folder for the class, called geog215, and save all of your work there, with subfolders for data, labs, and notes:
geog215/
├── data/
├── labs/
│   └── lab01.Rmd
└── notes/
Use short file names with no spaces, such as lab01.Rmd. Spaces and special characters in file names cause trouble in code, and a consistent naming pattern makes files easy to find.

text:
2.4 Code basics
The rest of this chapter introduces five ideas that appear in every R script: lines, blocks, variables, comments, and functions. A cooking analogy runs through all of them (Table 2.3).



Table 2.3: Code ideas and their cooking analogies.





Code
Cooking analogy




A line of code
One step in a recipe


A block of code
A recipe: several steps that make one dish


A program
A full meal: several recipes combined


A function
An appliance: ingredients go in, a dish comes out






The code boxes in the rest of this chapter are live. Click Run Code to run the R inside them, right here in your browser. You can also edit the code and run it again, which is the best way to learn what each piece does. The first time you run a box, R takes a few seconds to load.

2.4.1 A line of code
Every program starts with one line of code, and every line does something. When you run a line, R evaluates it and returns the result. Try it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
R returns 11, again with [1] in front to mark the first element of the result. A single line is like a single step in a recipe: “chop the onion,” or “add 5 and 6.”
Sometimes a line produces no visible result. Storing a value in a variable, which you will see below, prints nothing at all. The line still did something, though. It changed what R is holding in memory.


2.4.2 A block of code
A block of code is a sequence of lines that work together on one related task, the way the steps of a recipe work together to make one dish. In an R Markdown file, a block usually lives in one code chunk. Here is a block that answers a question: how many months are in a century?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The block stores 12 in months, stores 100 in years, multiplies them, and prints the answer, 1200. Its first line starts with #, which makes it a comment, covered below.


2.4.3 Variables
A variable is a named piece of memory that holds data. Once a value is stored in a variable, you can reuse it by name instead of typing it again.
You store a value with the assignment operator, <-, which looks like an arrow pointing left. The value on the right is stored in the name on the left. Read it out loud as “gets”: months <- 12 is “months gets 12.” In RStudio, the shortcut Alt+- (Option+- on a Mac) types the arrow for you.
Variable names are case-sensitive: Months and months are two different variables. Run this box, which asks for Months with a capital M:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
R replies with an error, object 'Months' not found, because no variable has exactly that name. This is one of the most common errors you will see, and now you know how to read it. Change Months to months and run the box again.
When you run code in RStudio, each new variable appears in the Environment pane. Checking that pane after you run a line is a good way to confirm that the line did what you meant.


2.4.4 Comments
A comment is a note for people, not for R. A comment begins with #, and R ignores everything after the # on that line. In the century example above, R skipped # How many months are in a century?, but a reader knows straight away what the block is for.
Use comments to explain why your code does what it does, not just what it does. The code itself already says that months * years multiplies two numbers. A good comment says why you needed that number. When you return to an assignment weeks later, comments are what let you understand your own reasoning, and in this course they are also how your instructor sees it.


2.4.5 Functions
A function takes inputs, does a job, and returns an output. The inputs are called arguments, and they go inside parentheses after the function’s name. If variables are the nouns of R, functions are the verbs.
In the cooking analogy, a function is an appliance, such as an oven. To make a pizza, you put bread, cheese, and tomato sauce into the oven, and the oven returns a pizza (Figure 2.4).







flowchart LR
  A["bread"] --> D{{"bake()"}}
  B["cheese"] --> D
  C["tomato_sauce"] --> D
  D --> E["pizza"]




Figure 2.4: A function takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output. In R this would be written pizza <- bake(bread, cheese, tomato_sauce).





In R, that would be written:
pizza <- bake(bread, cheese, tomato_sauce)
Here bake() is the function; bread, cheese, and tomato_sauce are the arguments; and the result is stored in a new variable, pizza. (bake() isn’t a real R function, but the pattern is exactly the one every real function follows.)
R comes with hundreds of real functions, and packages add thousands more. Run this box to try a few:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
c() is itself a function: it combines values into a vector, a sequence of values that R stores together. mean() and max() each take a vector and return one number. The last line converts the average to degrees Celsius. It nests one function inside another, so mean() runs first and round() rounds its result, and it shows a named argument, digits = 1, which tells round() how many decimal places to keep. Every function has a help page that lists its arguments; type ?round in the Console to see one in the Help pane.


2.4.6 Chaining functions with the pipe
Nested functions like the last line above are read from the inside out, which gets hard to follow as they grow. The pipe operator, |>, lets you write the same steps from left to right instead. The pipe takes the result on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This gives the same answer as round(sqrt(max(temps)), digits = 1), but reads in the order the steps happen. Read the pipe out loud as “and then”: take temps, and then find the maximum, and then take its square root, and then round it to one decimal place. You will use the pipe constantly in later chapters to string together steps that clean, analyze, and map data, and it is required in the course’s assignments.


2.4.7 A program
A program is a set of lines and blocks of code that work together to do a task, the way several recipes combine into a full meal. Every assignment in this course is a program: an R Markdown file that loads data, analyzes it, and makes a map.
R runs a program from top to bottom, so order matters. A variable must be created before it is used. When you work interactively, it is easy to run chunks out of order, or to delete a line that created a variable that is still sitting in your Environment. Everything seems to work until you knit, and then the fresh session that knitting starts in reports object not found. That error is doing you a favor: it means your file, as written, would not have worked for anyone else either.

2.5 Some hints for coding
Two habits make the biggest difference when you start writing code.
Think about the syntax. R is exact. Spelling, capital letters, commas, quotation marks, and brackets all have to be right, and every opening parenthesis needs a closing one. A single missing comma is enough to stop a program. When something fails, check the syntax of the line the error points to first.
Think about the purpose. Before you type a line, say in plain words what it should do: “store the number of years,” “find the average temperature.” If you can’t say it, you aren’t ready to write it yet. If you can, the words make a good comment.
And leave lots of comments. They are notes to Future You, who will not remember, three weeks from now, why you wrote that line.

title: 2  R, RStudio, and R Markdown
text:
2.8 Summary

R is the language that does the computing. RStudio is the workspace where you write and run R. R Markdown is the document format that combines your writing with your code and its results.
RStudio has four panes: the Editor for writing and saving code, the Console for running commands and reading output, the Environment for the variables in memory, and Files, Plots, and Help.
An R Markdown file has a YAML header, Markdown text, and code chunks. Knitting reruns every chunk from the top in a fresh session and builds a finished report, which is what makes the work reproducible.
A line of code does one thing; a block of lines does one task; a program combines blocks to do a whole job, and runs from top to bottom.
Variables store values with <- and are case-sensitive. Comments start with # and are notes for people. Functions take arguments and return an output, and the pipe |> chains them from left to right.
Keep all course files in one folder, mind your syntax, and comment generously.

title: 3  R Basics
text:
3.1 How R runs your code
The last chapter introduced R, RStudio, and R Markdown, and the building blocks of a line of code. This chapter moves from reading code to writing it. It covers four things you will rely on in every assignment: how R actually runs your code, how to add new abilities to R with packages, how R stores different kinds of values, and what to do when something goes wrong.
None of it is spatial yet. But every map and every analysis later in the book is built from these pieces, and most of the problems students hit in the first weeks of the course come from one of them: chunks run out of order, a package that was never loaded, a number stored as text, or an error message nobody read.
crumbs: 3  R Basics

title: 3  R Basics
text:
3.1.1 R is an interpreted language
R is an interpreted language. An interpreter is a program that executes instructions directly, one line at a time: it reads a line of code, translates it into something the computer can act on, runs it, and then moves on to the next line.
Other languages, such as C or Java, use a compiler instead. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before any of it runs. A good analogy is translation at a conference. An interpreter is like a live translator who translates the speaker sentence by sentence, as the speech happens. A compiler is like a book translator, who translates the whole book before anyone reads a page.
Being interpreted is what makes R so good for exploring data. You can run a single line, look at the result, and decide what to do next, without building and running a whole program. That is exactly what you do in RStudio every time you press Ctrl+Enter.


3.1.2 Order matters
The flip side is that R only knows what you have run so far, in the order you ran it. Nothing stops you from running the chunks of an R Markdown file out of order, and when you do, the same code can leave a different result.
Here are three chunks. Each one stores a different number in a variable called day.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
And here is a chunk that prints whatever day holds right now:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Run the three chunks top to bottom, then run the last one: day is 3. Now run the second chunk again, and then the last one: day is 2. The code in the file hasn’t changed, but the value in memory has, because R keeps whichever value it was given most recently. Before you click, try to predict what day will be.
In RStudio, the Environment pane always shows the current value of every variable, so it is the place to check what R is holding at any moment.


3.1.3 Knitting runs everything again
Out-of-order code is a quiet problem while you work, and a loud one when you knit. As the last chapter explained, knitting starts a fresh R session and runs every chunk from the top of the file to the bottom. If your file only worked because you ran chunk 5 before chunk 3, or because a variable you made in the Console is still sitting in the Environment, the knit fails. This is the most common reason an assignment won’t knit.


3.1.4 Rule one: think sequentially
The fix is a habit, and it is the first rule of this course: think sequentially.

Run your code in order, top to bottom, at least while you are learning.
Check the Environment pane to see which variables exist and what they hold.
Every so often, choose Run > Restart R and Run All Chunks (Figure 3.1). This clears memory and reruns the whole file from the top, the same way knitting does. If it works, your file will knit.







Figure 3.1: The Run menu at the top of the RStudio Editor. Restart R and Run All Chunks reruns the whole file in a fresh session, as knitting does.

title: 3  R Basics
text:
3.2 Packages and libraries

3.2.1 What is a package?
Base R, the R you get when you install it, can do arithmetic, statistics, and basic plots. Almost everything else reaches you through packages. A package bundles functions, data, and documentation that someone else has written and tested, and that you can add to your own copy of R. A useful comparison is a car: base R is the engine, and packages are the add-ons, like GPS or a sunroof. In this course you will use the tidyverse for cleaning data, sf for spatial data, and tmap for maps, all of them packages.
Packages are worth using for four reasons:

They save you from reinventing the wheel. Why write your own code for a complex task when an expert has already written, tested, and documented a function for it?
They give you specialized tools for particular fields, from spatial analysis to genomics to finance.
They are often faster than code you would write yourself, because they are optimized for speed and memory.
They make your work reproducible. Anyone who installs the same packages can rerun your analysis.



3.2.2 Packages versus libraries
The words package and library are often used as if they meant the same thing, but there is a difference:

A package is the bundle itself: the collection of code, data, and documentation.
A library is the folder on your computer where installed packages are stored. You can have more than one.

You install a package into a library. Then, confusingly, you load it with a function called library(). In casual conversation people say “the tidyverse library,” and that’s fine, but it helps to know which is which.


3.2.3 CRAN
Most packages come from CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. CRAN is the official repository for R packages: think of it as R’s app store. It hosts thousands of packages, and each one passes a set of quality checks before it is published. You may later meet other sources, such as Bioconductor for genomics packages or GitHub for development versions, but everything in this course comes from CRAN.


3.2.4 Install once, load every session
Using a package takes two steps, and the difference between them matters (Table 3.1).



Table 3.1: Installing a package compared with loading it.











Install
Load




What it does
Downloads the package into your library
Makes the package’s functions available right now


How often
Once per computer (and again to update)
Every R session


How
RStudio’s Packages tab, or install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)


Quotes?
Yes, around the package name
No


Belongs in your .Rmd file?
No
Yes, at the top






Installing downloads the package from CRAN and saves it in your library. You can do it with code, install.packages("tidyverse"), but in this course please use RStudio instead: open the Packages tab in the bottom-right pane, click Install, type the package name, and click Install again (Figure 3.2). Either way, you only need to do it once on each computer.






Figure 3.2: The Packages tab in RStudio’s bottom-right pane. Click Install to download a new package from CRAN. The list below shows the packages already installed in your library.



Never leave install.packages() in an R Markdown file. Knitting runs every line, so the file would download and reinstall the package every single time you knit.
Loading makes an installed package’s functions available in the current session. Put a library() call for each package you need at the top of every R Markdown file:
library(tidyverse)
You need to load packages every time, because every R session, including the fresh one that knitting starts, begins with no packages loaded. Notice that library() doesn’t need quotation marks around the package name, while install.packages() does. That small difference trips up a lot of people.
If a file calls library() for a package that isn’t installed, R stops with an error like there is no package called 'tidyverse'. RStudio also tries to help: when you open a file that uses a package you don’t have, a yellow bar at the top of the Editor offers to install it for you.

title: 3  R Basics
text:
3.3 Data types
Before you can analyze data, you need to know how R stores it. This section covers variables, vectors, and the four basic kinds of values R works with.

3.3.1 Variables, again
Recall from the last chapter that a variable is a named piece of data in memory, and that the assignment operator <- puts the value on its right into the name on its left:
# a character (text) variable
myName <- "Harry Potter"
Read it out loud as “myName gets "Harry Potter".” In R we (usually) assign from right to left. The name always goes on the left of the arrow and the value on the right. "Harry Potter" -> myName also works, but it is easy to misread, so don’t use it.


3.3.2 Vectors
The most basic data structure in R is the vector: a sequence of values that all have the same data type. You make one with c(), short for combine:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Even a single value is a vector, with a length of one. That is why R prints [1] in front of 5 + 6: the answer is the first (and only) element of a vector. It is also why so many R functions work on whole vectors at once. temps * 2 doubles every temperature, with no loop required.


3.3.3 The four atomic data types
R has four main atomic data types, the basic kinds of values a vector can hold (Table 3.2).



Table 3.2: R’s four main atomic data types.










Type
What it stores
Example




logical
TRUE or FALSE
isHot <- TRUE


integer
Whole numbers
myAge <- 21L


numeric
Numbers that can have decimals
myAccount <- 103.21


character
Text, always in quotation marks
myName <- "Harry Potter"







Logical values are TRUE and FALSE, written in capitals with no quotation marks. They are the answers to yes-or-no questions such as “is it raining?” or “is this county’s income above the median?” The next chapter uses them to pick out data.
Integer values are whole numbers. One detail surprises people: R stores a number you type, such as 21, as numeric unless you add an L to the end, as in 21L. In practice you rarely need to care; R converts between integers and numerics for you.
Numeric values (also called doubles) are numbers that can have a decimal part, such as temperatures, incomes, or coordinates. Most numbers you work with will be numeric.
Character values are text, also called strings. They always go inside quotation marks, which is how R tells the text "Durham" apart from a variable named Durham.

The function class() tells you what type a value is. Run this box, then try changing the values:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


3.3.4 One type per vector
Because a vector holds values of a single type, mixing types forces R to convert some of them. This conversion is called coercion, and R picks the type that can hold everything without losing information. Text can hold anything, so if a vector contains even one character value, the whole vector becomes character:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The numbers have all turned into text (notice the quotation marks), and mean() can no longer average them. It returns NA with a warning. This is a very common source of trouble with real data: one stray letter or symbol in a column of numbers, such as "N/A" or "12,000", turns the entire column into text. When a calculation gives an odd result, class() is one of the first things to check.


3.3.5 Naming variables
Variable names can’t contain spaces, so names made of several words need a convention. Two are common (Table 3.3).



Table 3.3: Two conventions for naming variables.










Convention
How it works
Examples




camelCase
Join the words; capitalize every word after the first
whatIsTheTemp, popChapelHill


snake_case
Lowercase words joined by underscores
what_is_the_temp, pop_chapel_hill






The tidyverse’s style guide uses snake_case, and so do most of the packages you will use. Either is fine in this course, as long as you pick one and use it consistently. Remember that names are case-sensitive, so popChapelHill and popchapelhill are different variables, and a file that mixes conventions is an easy place for that kind of typo to hide.
Whichever convention you use, choose names that say what the variable holds. popChapelHill tells a reader something; x or data2 does not. Short abbreviations, such as popCH, are fine if they are clear in context.

text:
3.4 Debugging and getting help

3.4.1 Mistakes are a fact of life
Everyone’s code breaks, including the code of people who have programmed for decades. A helpful way to think about errors is as puzzles to solve, not failures. Each one is a chance to understand the code, the language, and the problem a little better, so the time you spend debugging is an investment in your skills, not time wasted. If you get stuck, that is part of learning to program, and it gets easier with practice.
When something breaks, work through it in order:

Read the error message, word by word. It usually says what went wrong, and often names the object or line involved.
Find the line that caused it. In a knit, the error names the chunk.
Make a guess about the cause, change one thing, and run the code again.



3.4.2 The most common mistakes
Three mistakes account for most of the problems students run into early in the course. Check for these first.

Not programming sequentially, and then being surprised when the file won’t knit (Section 3.1).
Not storing files consistently, for example working straight out of the Downloads folder, so that R can’t find the data.
Missing parentheses, commas, and quotation marks. One missing ) or " is enough to stop a program.

The second one has a simple fix. For now, save all of the files for an assignment in the same folder, inside your geog215 folder. When you knit, the HTML file appears in that folder; when you download data, save it there too. Then R will find everything. Don’t use the Desktop or Downloads folders as a place to work.


3.4.3 Getting help with a function
If you aren’t sure what a function does, or what arguments it takes, open its help page. Either of these works:
help(mean)
?mean
The help page opens in the Help tab of the bottom-right pane (Figure 3.3). Every help page has the same layout: a Description of what the function does, its Usage (how to call it, with each argument’s default value), a list of Arguments, and, at the bottom, Examples you can copy and run. The examples are often the quickest way to understand a function.






Figure 3.3: A help page in RStudio’s Help tab, for the function download.file(). Every help page has the same sections: Description, Usage, Arguments, and Examples further down.





3.4.4 Getting help with an error
If you don’t understand an error message, copy it into a search engine. Someone has almost always run into the same error before, and the answer is often on Stack Overflow or the Posit Community forum. Leave out the parts that are specific to you, such as your variable names, so the search matches other people’s posts.


3.4.5 Using AI in this course
You may use AI tools such as Copilot to help explain an error message. For example, given the line my_age -> 39, an AI tool can point out that the assignment arrow is backwards and that you meant my_age <- 39. Use the explanation to understand the fix, then make the change yourself.
Don’t use AI to write your code. Generated code is often buggy, it often doesn’t follow the course’s coding standards (code that doesn’t won’t receive credit), and, most importantly, the point is for you to learn to write R yourself.


3.4.6 Getting help from people
In GEOG 215 there are three ways to get help from the teaching team:

Post in the Help! channel in the course’s Microsoft Teams team. The TAs and the instructor check it daily, and your classmates can learn from the answer too.
Come to office hours, in person or online, with the instructor or a TA.
Email the instructor for anything private, such as grades or accommodations.

When you ask, include the code you ran and the full error message. “My code doesn’t work” is hard to answer; “library(tidyverse) gives there is no package called 'tidyverse'” can be answered in one line.

title: 3  R Basics
text:
3.6 Summary

R is an interpreted language: it runs one line at a time, in the order you run it. The same chunks run in a different order can leave different values in memory.
Knitting reruns every chunk from the top in a fresh session. Think sequentially, check the Environment pane, and use Restart R and Run All Chunks to make sure your file will knit.
A package is a bundle of code written by others; a library is the folder where installed packages live. Most packages come from CRAN.
Install a package once per computer, with the Packages tab. Load it in every session with library(), at the top of every R Markdown file. Never put install.packages() in an .Rmd file.
A vector is a sequence of values of one type, made with c(). R’s four atomic types are logical, integer, numeric, and character; class() tells you which one you have. Mixing types coerces the whole vector, usually to character.
Name variables in camelCase or snake_case, consistently, with names that say what they hold.
Errors are normal. Read the message, find the line, and check the common mistakes first. For help, use ?function, search the error, and ask on Teams or in office hours. Use AI to explain errors, not to write your code.

4.1 A vector to work with
So far you have created values and stored them in variables. Most of the work of data analysis, though, is not creating data but picking out the part of it you need: the counties with incomes above the state median, the flights that left LaGuardia in June, the census tracts inside one city. Selecting part of a vector or table is called indexing, and it is the subject of this chapter.
We start with vectors, which you met in the last chapter, and three ways to index them: by position, by a logical condition, and by name. Then we stack vectors side by side into a data frame, R’s table, and finish by reading a table from a file.
Most of the examples in this chapter use one vector, called vect, which holds ten numbers between 1 and 1000:
Each element of a vector has a position, called its index. Table 4.1 shows each value above its index. Notice that R starts counting at 1, not 0 as some other languages do: the first element is at index 1.
To index a vector, put square brackets after its name. What you put inside the brackets decides which elements come back, and there are three choices:
The live code boxes in this chapter share one R session, so run the box above first to create vect. As you read, try to predict each answer before you run the code.

4.3.1 Comparisons return TRUE or FALSE

Read vect[vect > 10] out loud as “the elements of vect where vect is greater than 10.” This is the single most useful idea in the chapter. Selecting the counties whose income is above the median, or the flights that left late, works exactly the same way.


4.3.4 Logical vectors are recycled
What if the logical vector is shorter than the vector you are indexing? R recycles it, repeating it until it is long enough. Here c(TRUE, FALSE) becomes TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, ..., ten values in all:

4.3.5 Combining conditions: AND, OR, and NOT
Often you need two conditions at once: values greater than 10 and less than 500, say. R has three logical operators for combining TRUE and FALSE values.
AND (&) is TRUE only when both sides are TRUE. Is the statement “the sun rises in the west AND humans breathe oxygen” true? No: the first part is false, so the whole statement is false.

4.5 Data frames

4.5.1 From one dimension to two
A vector is one-dimensional: a single row of values. Stand several vectors of the same length side by side, and you get a two-dimensional table. In R, that table is a data frame, and it is how R stores almost every data set you will work with, including, later in the course, spatial data.
A data frame is organized into rows and columns (Table 4.7):

Each column is a variable: something measured or recorded, such as a name or an exam score.
Each row is an observation: one thing that was measured, such as a student, a county, or a flight.
All the values in a column must have the same data type. Each column is a vector, and, as you saw in the last chapter, a vector holds just one type. Different columns can have different types.

Here name and exam1 are character columns, exam2 is numeric, and bonus is logical. Suppose a number, such as 75.4, crept into the exam1 column of letter grades. R would not keep a number in a character column: it would coerce the 75.4 into the text "75.4". The same thing happens in reverse, and causes more trouble: a single letter or symbol in a column of numbers, such as "N/A" in exam2, turns the whole column into text, and then you can no longer average it.


4.5.2 Creating a data frame
The function data.frame() builds a data frame from vectors. Each argument becomes a column: the name before = is the column name, and the vector after = holds its values. Every vector must be the same length, here four:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Here is another data frame:

  x = 1:5,
  y = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")
)
What are its column names? Is df a good name for a data frame? Are x and y good names for its columns? Neither tells a reader anything about the data. Prefer descriptive names, such as grades or nc_counties, and add a comment saying what the data frame holds and where it came from.




4.5.3 Looking at a data frame
A few functions tell you what is in a data frame without printing all of it, which matters once a data frame has thousands of rows:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
In RStudio, View(grades) also opens the data frame in a spreadsheet-like tab, and clicking a data frame’s name in the Environment pane does the same.


4.5.4 Indexing a data frame
The same bracket indexing works on data frames, with one change: a data frame has two dimensions, so the brackets take two indexes, separated by a comma. The row comes first, then the column: grades[row, column].

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Leaving a position blank means “all of them,” so grades[2, ] is the whole second row and grades[, "exam2"] is the whole exam2 column. Don’t forget the comma: without it, R treats the number as a column index, not a row.
Because pulling out one column is so common, R has a shortcut, the dollar sign. grades$exam2 returns the exam2 column as a vector, which you can then use like any other vector:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Everything from earlier in the chapter now applies to rows. Put a condition in the row position, and you get the rows where it is TRUE:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The first line returns the two students who scored over 90 on exam 2. The second returns the names of the students who earned the bonus and an A on exam 1. In the next chapter you will meet filter(), the tidyverse’s way to do the same thing with less typing.

4.6 Reading tabular data
You will rarely type a data set in by hand. Usually it arrives as a file, and the most common format is a CSV file (comma-separated values): plain text in which each line is a row and commas separate the values. The first line usually holds the column names, called the header. Here is the grades table as a CSV file:
name,exam1,exam2,bonus
Eliza,A,98.1,TRUE
Shonda,A-,85.4,TRUE

Base R has two functions for reading text files like this into a data frame.
read.table() is the general-purpose workhorse. It reads any table of text in which the values are separated by some character, called the delimiter, and it has many options, including:

sep: the delimiter, such as "," for commas or "\t" for tabs.

scores <- read.csv("scores.csv")
Its sibling read.csv2() reads the kind of CSV file common in much of Europe, which uses a comma as the decimal mark (3,14) and a semicolon to separate values.
Remember from Section 3.4 that R looks for the file relative to the folder your .Rmd file is saved in. If the CSV file is in the same folder, the file name alone is enough; if it is in a data subfolder, write read.csv("data/scores.csv"). Most “cannot open file” errors are file path errors.

title: 4  Indexing Vectors and Data Frames
text:
4.8 Summary

Indexing selects part of a vector or table, with square brackets. R counts positions from 1.
By position: vect[3] is the value at position 3; vect[-3] drops it; vect[c(1, 3)] and vect[6:8] return several values. The colon operator : makes a sequence.
Comparison operators (>, <, >=, <=, ==, !=) return TRUE or FALSE for every element. Equality is ==; a single = sets an argument.
By condition: vect[vect > 10] keeps the elements where the condition is TRUE. Combine conditions with & (AND: both must be true), | (OR: either can be true), and ! (NOT). Short logical vectors are recycled.
By name: names() labels the elements, and vect["Fozzie"] selects by label. length() counts elements, and vect[length(vect)] is the last one.
A data frame is a table of equal-length vectors: columns are variables, rows are observations, and each column holds one data type. Make one with data.frame(), and index it with df[row, column] or df$column.
Read CSV files with read.csv() (or read.table() for other delimiters), and check the column types after you read.

text:
5.1 What is the tidyverse?
In the last chapter you selected rows of a data frame with square brackets, as in grades[grades$exam2 > 90, ]. That works, but it gets long and hard to read quickly: the data frame’s name appears again for every condition, and every step needs a new variable. This chapter introduces the tidyverse, a set of packages designed to make that kind of work shorter and easier to read, and three tools from it that you will use in almost every assignment from here on: glimpse() to see what is in a data frame, filter() to keep the rows you need, and the pipe, |>, to chain steps together.
The examples use real data: every flight that left New York City’s three airports in 2013, from the nycflights13 package. By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer questions such as “how many flights left LaGuardia in June?” in four short lines.

title: 5  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
5.1.1 The data science workflow
The tidyverse is a family of R packages built for data science. Its packages share a design philosophy, a grammar, and a way of storing data, so they fit together. They are organized around the workflow in Figure 5.1, from the book R for Data Science (Wickham et al. 2023):







flowchart LR
  A["Import"] --> B["Tidy"]
  B --> C
  subgraph C["Understand"]
    direction LR
    T["Transform"] --> V["Visualize"]
    V --> M["Model"]
    M --> T
  end
  C --> D["Communicate"]




Figure 5.1: The data science workflow, after Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund (2023). Data are imported and tidied, then transformed, visualized, and modeled, often several times over, before the results are communicated. This chapter is about tidying and transforming.





First you import data into R. Then you tidy it into a consistent shape, with one variable per column and one observation per row. Then you go round a loop of transforming it (keeping the rows you need, making new columns, summarizing), visualizing it, and modeling it, until you understand it. Finally you communicate what you found, usually in an R Markdown report. This chapter lives in the Tidy and Transform boxes: getting data into shape and pulling out the rows you need.


5.1.2 The core packages
One command, install.packages("tidyverse") (or one trip to the Packages tab), installs the core tidyverse packages (Table 5.1).



Table 5.1: The core tidyverse packages.









Package
What it is for




dplyr
Transforming data frames: keeping rows, choosing columns, making new columns, summarizing


ggplot2
Plots and charts


tidyr
Reshaping data into a tidy form


readr
Reading files such as CSVs, with read_csv()


tibble
The tidyverse’s version of the data frame


stringr
Working with text


forcats
Working with categories (factors)


lubridate
Working with dates and times


purrr
Repeating a task over many inputs






This chapter uses dplyr, which supplies glimpse() and filter(). Posit publishes a one-page cheatsheet for dplyr, Data transformation with dplyr, linked on the course Canvas page and at https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/. filter() is on the front page under Manipulate Cases (Extract Cases). It is worth keeping open while you work.


5.1.3 Loading the tidyverse
Load the tidyverse at the top of every R Markdown file, the same way as any other package:
library(tidyverse)
The first time you do, R prints a block of messages like this (your version numbers may differ):
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.1.4     ✔ readr     2.1.5
✔ forcats   1.0.0     ✔ stringr   1.5.1
✔ ggplot2   3.5.1     ✔ tibble    3.2.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.3     ✔ tidyr     1.3.1
✔ purrr     1.0.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
These messages are normal. They are not errors, even though some are printed in red. The first block lists the packages that were loaded. The second, Conflicts, says that two packages contain a function with the same name, and which one R will use. Here, dplyr’s filter() masks the filter() in base R’s stats package (a function for time series). From now on, when you type filter(), you get dplyr’s version, which is the one you want. If you ever need the other one, you can name its package explicitly with two colons: stats::filter().


5.1.4 Tidying data is a set of verbs
What do we actually do when we tidy data? We select, extract, arrange, sort, combine, group, join, and summarize. dplyr gives each of these jobs its own function, named with a verb (Table 5.2).



Table 5.2: The main dplyr verbs.










dplyr verb
What it does
Covered




filter()
Keeps the rows that meet a condition
This chapter


select()

Next chapter


arrange()

Next chapter


mutate()

Next chapter


group_by() and summarize()

Later in the course






Every dplyr verb works the same way: its first argument is a data frame, the arguments after it say what to do, and it returns a new data frame. That consistency is what makes the pipe, later in this chapter, work so well.

5.2 Seeing inside a data frame with glimpse()

5.2.1 The flights data
The nycflights13 package contains a data frame called flights: one row for every flight that departed from New York City’s three airports (Newark, EWR; John F. Kennedy, JFK; and LaGuardia, LGA) in 2013. You might use it to compare flights by day, by airport, or by how late they left. Install it once from the Packages tab, then load it along with the tidyverse:

5.2.2 glimpse()
flights has more than 300,000 rows, far too many to print. Typing flights shows only the first few rows and as many columns as fit across the screen. glimpse() is the tidyverse’s way to see everything that is in a data frame at once. It turns the data on its side: each column becomes one line of output, showing the column’s name, its type, and its first few values. Run it:

In glimpse()

5.3 Keeping rows with filter()

5.3.1 One condition
filter() keeps the rows of a data frame that meet a condition. Its first argument is the data frame, and the arguments after that are one or more logical conditions:
filter(data, condition)
It returns only the rows where the condition is TRUE. Here are the flights that left on the first day of a month:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
flights is the data frame, and day == 1 is the logical condition. Notice that, inside filter(), you refer to the columns by name alone, day rather than flights$day: filter() knows to look for them in the data frame. The result has 11,036 rows, the flights on the 1st of each of the twelve months.
The condition uses ==, which tests whether two things are equal. A single = sets an argument, and writing filter(flights, day = 1) is one of the most common mistakes in R. dplyr catches it and tells you, with an error that says you have used = instead of == and asks “Did you mean day == 1?”
filter() doesn’t change flights; it returns a new data frame. To keep the result, store it with <-, and give it a new name, so that you still have the original:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


5.3.2 Several conditions
Give filter() more than one condition, separated by commas, and it keeps the rows where all of them are TRUE. A comma inside filter() means AND, exactly like &. These two lines both find the flights on January 1:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both return 842 rows. For OR, use |. This finds the flights in June or July:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Conditions on text work the same way, but the text needs quotation marks, as always: origin == "LGA", not origin == LGA. Without the quotes, R looks for a column or variable named LGA and doesn’t find one.

title: 5  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
5.4 The pipe

5.4.1 Chaining steps with |>
Most questions take several steps. Suppose you want to know how many flights left LaGuardia early, or on time, on January 1, 2013. That takes three filters and a count. You could save a new data frame after every step, or nest the functions inside one another, but both get hard to read.
You met the pipe, |>, in an earlier chapter. It takes the output of one function and feeds it in as the first argument of the next. Because every dplyr verb takes a data frame as its first argument and returns one, verbs can be chained with pipes as long as you like:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read the pipe out loud as “and then”: take flights, and then keep January 1, and then keep LaGuardia, and then keep the flights that left on time or early (a delay of zero or less), and then count the rows. The answer is 172 flights. Each step narrows the rows further, and the code reads in the same order as the question.


5.4.2 Don’t repeat the data frame
With the pipe, the data frame goes in front of the pipe, not inside filter(). These two lines do exactly the same thing:
filter(flights, day == 1)
flights |> filter(day == 1)
In the second, |> passes flights into filter() as its first argument. So inside a pipe chain you never write filter(flights, ...). If you do, flights is passed in twice, once by the pipe and once by you, and R reports an error.






TipThis is not a pipe



René Magritte’s 1929 painting The Treachery of Images shows a pipe above the words Ceci n’est pas une pipe, “This is not a pipe.” It isn’t: it’s a picture of one. In the same spirit, |> isn’t really a pipe either. It’s an operator, a piece of R grammar that rewrites x |> f(y) as f(x, y) before the code runs. The plumbing metaphor is just a good way to picture it: data flow in at one end and out at the other.
You may also see %>% in older code and online answers. It is the original pipe, from the magrittr package (named after Magritte), and does almost the same job. The native pipe |> was added to R itself in version 4.1, and it is the one this course requires.

text:
5.5 Missing values: why the counts don’t match

5.5.1 The same question, two ways
Here is the January 1 LaGuardia question again, answered first with base R brackets, as in the last chapter, and then the tidy way with filter() and the pipe:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The base R way needs more typing, and more places for a typo: flights$ for every condition, and a new object at every step. The tidy way reads top to bottom. But look at the answers. Base R finds 174 flights, and filter() finds 172. They don’t match. Why?


5.5.2 NA: a missing value
The answer is missing values. In R, a value that is unknown or missing is written NA (“not available”). Flights that were cancelled never departed, so their departure delay is unknown: dep_delay is NA. Two of the January 1 LaGuardia flights were cancelled.
What is NA <= 0? R can’t say whether an unknown number is less than zero, so the answer is itself unknown: NA, not TRUE or FALSE. Each approach handles that differently (Table 5.4):

Base R brackets don’t drop a row when the condition is NA. They return a row in which every value is NA, so the result has two extra rows of missing values, 174 in all.
filter() keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE. It quietly drops rows where the condition is NA, so it finds 172.




Table 5.4: How base R brackets and filter() treat each result of a condition.












Condition is TRUE
Condition is FALSE
Condition is NA




Base R df[condition, ]
Row kept
Row dropped
A row of NAs is returned


filter(df, condition)
Row kept
Row dropped
Row dropped






You can see the two extra rows by looking at the last rows of the base R result:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


5.5.3 Deciding what happens to NAs
Neither approach is wrong, but they give different answers, and nothing warns you. That is annoying, and it is exactly the kind of quiet difference that leads to wrong results in a report. The lesson is to check the number of rows after every filter, and to decide on purpose what should happen to missing values.
If you do want to keep the rows with a missing delay, say so in the condition, with the function is.na(), which returns TRUE when a value is NA:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read the second filter as “keep the flight if its delay is missing or it left on time or early.” Now filter() also returns 174. To count the missing values themselves, filter for them: filter(flights, is.na(dep_delay)) returns all 8,255 flights in 2013 with no departure delay recorded.
Note that you can’t test for NA with ==. dep_delay == NA is always NA, whatever dep_delay is, because R can’t tell whether something equals an unknown value. Always use is.na().

5.6 Practice: counting flights
Put it all together. These steps follow the in-class exercise.
Step 1: set up. In RStudio, use the Packages tab to install nycflights13 and tidyverse, if you haven’t yet. Start a new R Markdown file, and load both in the first chunk:
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
You will see the tidyverse’s startup messages. Remember that they are not errors.
Step 2: count all the flights. The dplyr function count() counts the rows of a data frame, so pipe flights into it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
There were 336,776 flights from New York City’s airports in 2013.
Step 3: flights in June. Add a filter() before count() that keeps month 6. Remember that month is stored as a number, so write 6, not "June". Try it before you look at the answer:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 3

flights |>
  filter(month == 6) |>
  count()
There were 28,243 flights in June.

Step 4: June flights from LaGuardia. Now keep only the June flights that left from LaGuardia. LaGuardia’s airport code is "LGA", and it is text, so it needs quotation marks. You can add a second filter(), or put both conditions in one, joined with a comma or &:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 4

All three of these return the same count, 8,596 flights. Pick the one you find easiest to read.
# Two filters, one after the other
flights |>
  filter(month == 6) |>
  filter(origin == "LGA") |>
  count()

# One filter, with a comma (AND)
flights |>
  filter(month == 6, origin == "LGA") |>
  count()

# One filter, with & (AND)
flights |>
  filter(month == 6 & origin == "LGA") |>
  count()
Read the first version as “take flights, and then keep June, and then keep LGA, and then count.” If you got a much bigger number, check for missing quotation marks around "LGA", or a single = where you need ==.

5.8 Summary

The tidyverse is a family of packages for data science that work together, organized around the workflow import, tidy, transform, visualize, model, and communicate. Load it with library(tidyverse); the startup and conflict messages are normal.
dplyr gives each data-tidying job a verb. Every verb takes a data frame first and returns a data frame.
glimpse() shows a data frame’s size and every column’s name, type (<int>, <dbl>, <chr>, <dttm>), and first values. Look at every data frame before you work with it.
filter() keeps the rows where a condition is TRUE. Use == to test equality, quotation marks around text, and commas or & for AND, | for OR.
The pipe |> passes the result on its left into the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then.” Inside a pipe chain, don’t repeat the data frame.
NA marks a missing value. Base R brackets return a row of NAs when a condition is NA; filter() drops it. Check row counts, and use is.na() when you want to keep or find missing values.

title: 6  Census Data and APIs
text:
6.1 A brief history of the US Census
Most of the spatial data science you will do about people in the United States starts with Census data. Population, income, housing, commuting, education: if a question involves who lives where, the Census Bureau has probably measured it, for small areas, across the whole country, for free.
This chapter has two halves. The first covers what the data are: where they come from, how Census geography is organized, and which variables you will use most. The second covers how to get them: what an API is, how to make a request by hand, and how the tidycensus package turns that request into one line of R that returns a map-ready data frame.
Article I of the Constitution requires a count of the population every ten years so that seats in the House of Representatives can be apportioned among the states. The first census, in 1790, was carried out by U.S. marshals on horseback and counted 3.9 million people. The count has run every decade since.
The Census Bureau has repeatedly pushed new technology into being because the job of counting a growing country kept outgrowing the old tools (Table 6.1). Herman Hollerith’s punch-card tabulating machines, built for the 1890 census, led to the company that became IBM. A century later, the 1990 census introduced TIGER, one of the first national digital map databases. The boundary files you will download later in this chapter descend directly from it.
For our purposes the most important change is the one from 2005. Before then, detailed social and economic questions (income, education, commuting) were asked on a “long form” sent to a sample of households once a decade. Since 2005 those questions have moved to the American Community Survey, which samples households every year. That gives two distinct sources of Census data, and you will choose between them constantly:

The decennial census is a full count of everyone, every ten years. It asks only a few questions (age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, household relationship, housing tenure), but it covers every person.
The American Community Survey (ACS) is a continuous sample survey. It asks many more questions, but every number it publishes is an estimate, with a margin of error (Section 6.7.1).


6.1.1 The moving center of population
Each census, the Bureau calculates the mean center of population: the point where a flat map of the United States would balance if every resident weighed the same. In 1790 it sat in Kent County, Maryland, on the Eastern Shore. By 2020 it had moved about 884 miles, in a straight line, to Wright County, Missouri (Figure 6.1) (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.).

lower48 <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m", year = 2020) |>
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI", "PR")) |>
  st_transform(5070)

# Draw each series as its own path, plus a dashed link between the two 1950 points
paths <- centers |>
  group_by(extent) |>
  summarize(do_union = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

link_1950 <- centers |>
  filter(year == 1950) |>
  summarize(do_union = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

labeled <- centers |>
  filter(year %in% c(1790, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2020), extent == "Lower 48" | year == 2020)

# Zoom to the eastern two-thirds of the country, where the path lies
zoom <- st_bbox(st_buffer(centers, 600000))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = lower48, fill = "#f6efe0", color = "#b9ad97", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = link_1950, color = "#3b5b7a", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = paths, color = "#3b5b7a", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = centers, aes(fill = year), shape = 21, size = 2.6, color = "white", stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_sf_label(
    data = labeled, aes(label = year), nudge_y = 75000,
    size = 3.2, label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.8)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9fb7cc", high = "#1d3550", name = "Census year") +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = zoom[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"))







Figure 6.1: Mean center of US population at each census, 1790–2020. Centers through 1950 are for the lower 48 states; from 1950 on they include Alaska and Hawaii, which pulls the 1950 point slightly west and south (dashed link). Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Centers of Population, 1790–2020.





The path tells the story of American settlement. Through the 1800s the center moved almost straight west as settlement pushed across the continent, fastest before 1900. After 1950 it bent southwest as the Sun Belt grew, and it has been in Missouri since 1980.






TipThink about it



Which direction do you expect the center of population to move by 2030? What trends in migration, birth rates, or immigration would push it further west, further south, or back east?
