title: 6  Census Data and APIs
text:
6.2 Census geography
Census data are always published for areas, never for individual people or addresses. Understanding how those areas are defined, and how they fit together, is the first step in using the data well.






Figure 6.2: The standard hierarchy of Census geographic entities. The central spine, from the nation down to blocks, nests completely. The entities branching off it do not. Source: U.S. Census Bureau.



Figure 6.2 shows the standard hierarchy. The central spine runs from the nation to regions, divisions, states, counties, census tracts, block groups, and finally blocks. Every unit on the spine nests perfectly: each block lies inside exactly one block group, which lies inside exactly one tract, one county, and one state. That nesting is what makes the spine so useful. You can add blocks up to block groups, block groups to tracts, and so on, and never double-count anyone.
The geographies that branch off the spine, such as ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, places (cities and towns), and congressional districts, are built from blocks too, but they do not nest neatly inside counties or tracts. A ZIP code can cross county lines, and a city can include parts of several tracts. When you have a choice, work on the spine.
The three smallest units on the spine are the ones you will use most for local analysis. Figure 6.3 shows all three for Orange County, North Carolina.

orange_tracts <- tracts("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)
orange_bgs    <- block_groups("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)
orange_blocks <- blocks("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)

geo_levels <- bind_rows(
  orange_tracts |> transmute(level = "Tracts"),
  orange_bgs    |> transmute(level = "Block groups"),
  orange_blocks |> transmute(level = "Blocks")
) |>
  mutate(level = fct_inorder(level))

ggplot(geo_levels) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#f6efe0", color = "#3b5b7a", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~level) +
  theme_void()







Figure 6.3: Census tracts, block groups, and blocks in Orange County, North Carolina (2020 boundaries). Each level subdivides the one above it.





Census blocks are the smallest unit. A block is often a single city block bounded by streets, but blocks are bounded by any visible feature (railroads, streams, shorelines) and in rural areas can be large. Only the decennial census is published for blocks, and in 2020 block-level data carry the most differential-privacy noise (Section 6.7.3), so use them with care.
Block groups combine several blocks and usually hold 600 to 3,000 people. They are the smallest geography for which ACS 5-year estimates are published, which makes them the finest level available for most social and economic variables. That detail comes at a cost: block group estimates have large margins of error.
Census tracts combine block groups and typically hold 1,200 to 8,000 people, about 4,000 on average. They are drawn to be fairly similar in population and stable over time, which makes them the workhorse unit for neighborhood analysis. Their boundaries are still revised each decade, though, so comparisons across censuses take care (Section 6.7.4).

6.2.1 FIPS codes and GEOIDs
Every Census area has a unique identifier called a GEOID, built by stringing together FIPS codes (Federal Information Processing Standards codes) for each level of the hierarchy. FIPS codes are standard numeric IDs for states and counties: North Carolina is 37 and Orange County is 135.

title: 6  Census Data and APIs
text:
6.4 What is an API?
You could get any of the variables above by clicking through data.census.gov and downloading a CSV. For a one-off table that works. For anything you want to repeat, share, or scale up, it is far better to ask for the data from code, through an API.
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules for how one program asks another for data or services. Your R script is one program; the Census Bureau’s server is the other. Your script sends a request, and the server sends back data (Figure 6.4).







flowchart LR
  A["Your code<br/>(R script)"] -- "request" --> B{{"API"}}
  B -- "request" --> C["Their server<br/>(Census Bureau)"]
  C -- "data" --> B
  B -- "data" --> A




Figure 6.4: An API sits between your code and someone else’s server. Your code sends a request in an agreed format, and the server returns data.





A restaurant menu is a useful analogy. The menu lists what you can order and how to ask for it. You never see the kitchen, and you get back exactly what you ordered, as long as you ordered something on the menu.

6.4.1 Web APIs: URLs in, JSON out
Most data APIs on the web follow a style called REST. Three ideas cover almost everything you need:

Every dataset or service has its own web address, called an endpoint. The 2022 ACS 5-year data live at https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5.
Requests are ordinary HTTP requests, the same thing your browser sends when it loads a page. A GET request reads data; a POST request sends data. Data APIs mostly use GET.
Responses usually come back as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), structured text that R can turn into lists or data frames.



6.4.2 Anatomy of a request
A REST request is just a URL with two parts: the endpoint, which says which service to call, and the parameters, which say what you want from it. A ? separates the two, each parameter is written name=value, and an & separates parameters.
Here is a request to Esri’s geocoding service that looks up one address:
https://geocode.arcgis.com/arcgis/rest/services/World/GeocodeServer/findAddressCandidates?singleLine=380%20new%20york%20st%20redlands%20ca&f=pjson
Everything before the ? is the endpoint. singleLine is the address to look up (%20 is how a space is written inside a URL), and f=pjson asks for pretty-printed JSON. Paste that URL into a browser and you will see the JSON response.
Here is a Census API request with the same structure. It asks for median household income for every county in North Carolina:
https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5?get=NAME,B19013_001E&for=county:*&in=state:37
get lists the variables, for picks the geography (county:* means every county), and in limits the request to state 37, North Carolina.


6.4.3 Why use an API?
APIs take a little more setup than a download button. They pay that back in four ways:

Reproducible. Your script is an exact record of what you downloaded, so you, a classmate, or a reviewer can rerun it and get the same data.
Targeted. Parameters return only the variables and places you need.
Current. You pull fresh data each time you run the script, instead of keeping stale files around.
Scalable. One loop can request every state, or every year.

These benefits might not seem like much the first time you download a table. They matter the second time you need the same data, or when someone asks exactly how you got it.

6.5 Calling an API from R
There are two ways to call an API from R: build the request yourself, or use a package that wraps the API for you. It is worth seeing both, because a wrapper package won’t always exist.

6.5.1 Step 0: get and store a key
The Census API asks you to identify yourself with a free key. Request one at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html; it arrives by email within a few minutes. Then store it once:

tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR KEY HERE", install = TRUE)

install = TRUE writes the key to your .Renviron file as CENSUS_API_KEY, so R loads it at the start of every session. Restart R after you run this. From then on, your code reads the key with Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY").






WarningKeep keys out of your scripts



Never paste an API key directly into a script or Quarto document you might share or push to GitHub. Anyone who has your key can use it as you. Store it in .Renviron, which stays on your computer.

Here are steps 1 to 3 for the North Carolina income request, using httr2:

library(httr2)

resp <- request("https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5") |>
  req_url_query(
    get   = "NAME,B19013_001E",
    `for` = "county:*",
    `in`  = "state:37",
    key   = Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")
  ) |>
  req_perform()

nc_raw <- resp_body_json(resp, simplifyVector = TRUE)
head(nc_raw)

for and in are reserved words in R, so they need backticks when used as argument names. Look at what comes back: a matrix of text, with the column names in the first row and every value, including income, stored as a string. Step 4 starts with cleaning it:

colnames(nc_raw) <- nc_raw[1, ]

nc_manual <- as_tibble(nc_raw[-1, ]) |>
  transmute(
    GEOID  = paste0(state, county),
    NAME,
    income = as.numeric(B19013_001E)
  )

nc_manual



6.5.3 With a package: tidycensus
tidycensus (Walker and Herman, n.d.) does steps 1 through 3, and most of step 4, for you. This single call builds the same URL behind the scenes, sends it, and returns a tidy data frame:

nc_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2022
)

nc_income

The result has one row per county with GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate, and moe (margin of error) columns. The rest of this chapter uses tidycensus. Similar wrapper packages exist for other services: tigris for Census boundary files and arcpullr for Esri REST services, for example. When there is no package for the API you need, the httr2 pattern above will always work.

text:
6.6 Worked example: mapping young children in North Carolina
This section puts the pieces together. The goal is to map the share of each North Carolina census tract’s population that is under 5 years old.

6.6.1 Find the variables
load_variables() downloads the full list of variables for a dataset and year:

vars_acs5 <- load_variables(2022, "acs5", cache = TRUE)

vars_acs5 |>
  filter(str_detect(name, "^B01001_")) |>
  head(5)

The result has a name column (the code), a label describing the line, a concept naming the table, and the smallest geography it is published for. In RStudio, View(vars_acs5) opens it in a searchable viewer. You can also filter it in code, for example filter(vars_acs5, str_detect(concept, "SEX BY AGE")). cache = TRUE saves the list so it loads instantly next time.
Searching the labels shows that table B01001, Sex by Age, has what we need: the total (_001), males under 5 (_003), and females under 5 (_027).






WarningCheck the concept, not just the label



Many ACS tables come in lettered versions for single race groups. B01001A is Sex by Age (White Alone) and B01001B is Sex by Age (Black or African American Alone). Their lines have the same labels as B01001, so it is easy to grab the wrong one. Always check the concept column.




6.6.2 Download data with geometry
get_acs() with geometry = TRUE downloads the tract boundaries along with the data and joins them on GEOID, so the result is an sf object, ready to map:

nc_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(total    = "B01001_001",
                male_u5  = "B01001_003",
                female_u5 = "B01001_027"),
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2022,
  output    = "wide",
  geometry  = TRUE
)

nc_tracts

Naming the variables (total = "B01001_001") gives the output columns readable names. output = "wide" puts each variable in its own pair of columns: totalE and totalM for the estimate and margin of error, and so on.


6.6.3 Calculate and map
Now add the two under-5 counts, divide by the total, and map the result. moe_sum() and moe_prop() carry the margins of error through the calculation (Section 6.7.1):

nc_under5 <- nc_tracts |>
  mutate(
    under5E   = male_u5E + female_u5E,
    under5M   = map2_dbl(male_u5M, female_u5M, \(a, b) moe_sum(c(a, b))),
    pct_u5    = under5E / totalE * 100,
    pct_u5_moe = moe_prop(under5E, totalE, under5M, totalM) * 100
  )

tm_shape(nc_under5) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill       = "pct_u5",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "% under 5"),
    lwd        = 0.2
  )

A handful of tracts have no value. These are tracts where no one lives, such as national forests, military training areas, or open water, so the percentage would mean dividing by zero. Before you interpret the map, remember that each tract’s value is an estimate. Small tracts can have margins of error nearly as large as the estimate itself, so a single dark tract may reflect sampling noise as much as a real pattern.






NoteTry it



Change the code above to map the share of each county’s population that is 65 or older. You will need several lines of B01001 for each sex. Use load_variables() to find them.

text:
6.7 Going further with tidycensus
The worked example covers the most common case. This section covers what you need to know once you are past your first download.

6.7.1 Margins of error
Every ACS value is an estimate from a sample, and tidycensus returns a margin of error (moe) alongside each estimate. ACS margins of error use a 90% confidence level: there is a 90% chance that the true value lies within estimate ± moe.
The smaller the area, the smaller the sample behind it, and the larger the margin of error relative to the estimate. A useful way to judge reliability is the coefficient of variation (CV): the standard error as a percentage of the estimate. Divide the MOE by 1.645 to get the standard error, then divide by the estimate:
\[
CV = \frac{MOE / 1.645}{\text{estimate}} \times 100
\]

nc_income |>
  mutate(cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(cv)) |>
  head()

There is no single official cutoff, but a common rule of thumb treats estimates with a CV above about 30% as unreliable: report them with caution, or combine areas or years to get a larger sample (U.S. Census Bureau 2020).
When you combine estimates you must also combine their margins of error, and you can’t just add them. tidycensus provides functions for the standard formulas: moe_sum() for sums, moe_prop() for proportions, moe_ratio() for ratios, and moe_product() for products.


6.7.2 Calculating percentages
Raw counts mostly tell you where people live. A map of the number of renters looks a lot like a map of population. To compare places, convert counts to shares.
The summary_var argument adds a second variable, usually the table total, to every row as summary_est and summary_moe. That puts the numerator and denominator side by side, so the share is a single division:

nc_white <- get_acs(
  geography   = "county",
  variables   = "B02001_002",
  summary_var = "B02001_001",
  state       = "NC",
  year        = 2022
) |>
  mutate(
    pct     = estimate / summary_est * 100,
    pct_moe = moe_prop(estimate, summary_est, moe, summary_moe) * 100
  )

nc_white |> select(NAME, estimate, summary_est, pct, pct_moe)



6.7.3 Decennial Census data
get_decennial() works like get_acs() but pulls from the full-count decennial census. Because these are counts rather than sample estimates, there is no moe column. For 2020, choose the summary file with sumfile: "pl" for the redistricting counts (available down to blocks) or "dhc" for more detailed age, sex, household, and housing tables.

nc_pop <- get_decennial(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = "P1_001N",
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2020,
  sumfile   = "dhc"
)

nc_pop

“Full count” does not mean “exact.” To protect respondents’ privacy, the 2020 census applied differential privacy: carefully calibrated statistical noise added to published tables. The noise is negligible for states and counties but can be substantial for blocks, especially for small population groups. Treat individual block counts with caution, and aggregate blocks where you can.


6.7.4 Comparing across years
Change over time is one of the most interesting things to measure with Census data, and one of the easiest to get wrong. Four traps to watch for:

Boundaries change. Tract and block group boundaries are redrawn every ten years. A GEOID from 2010 and the same GEOID in 2020 may not describe the same place. ACS releases from 2020 on use 2020 boundaries.
5-year periods overlap. The 2017–2021 and 2018–2022 estimates share four years of responses, so differences between them are muted. Compare non-overlapping periods, such as 2013–2017 and 2018–2022.
Dollars are nominal. Income, rent, and home values are reported in dollars of their own period. Adjust for inflation before comparing.
Codes change. Tables and lines are occasionally renumbered or redefined. Check load_variables() for every year you use.

get_acs() returns one year per call. To pull several, loop over the years with purrr and stack the results:

years <- c(2012, 2017, 2022)  # non-overlapping 5-year periods

nc_income_years <- map(years, \(y) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = "B19013_001",
    state     = "NC",
    year      = y
  ) |>
    mutate(year = y)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

nc_income_years |> filter(NAME == "Orange County, North Carolina")

The 2012, 2017, and 2022 releases cover 2008–2012, 2013–2017, and 2018–2022, so they do not overlap. The income values are still in nominal dollars.


6.7.5 More tidycensus functions
tidycensus can do much more than get_acs() and get_decennial(). Table 6.6 lists some of the most useful extras.



Table 6.6: Other tidycensus functions and arguments.










Function or argument
What it returns
Example use




get_estimates()
Annual population estimates and components of change
County population growth since 2020


get_pums()
Individual and household ACS microdata
Custom tabulations not in published tables


get_flows()
County-to-county migration flows
Where people moving into a county came from


table = "B19001"
Every variable in one ACS table
Full household income distribution in one call


survey = "acs1"
1-year ACS estimates
Recent data for large counties and metros


tigris::erase_water()
Geometry with water areas removed
Cleaner maps along coasts and lakes

title: 6  Census Data and APIs
text:
6.8 Summary

US Census data come from two main sources: the decennial census, a full count every ten years with few questions, and the American Community Survey, a continuous sample with many questions and a margin of error on every estimate.
Census geography nests from the nation down to tracts, block groups, and blocks. Every area has a GEOID built from FIPS codes. Keep GEOIDs as text and join on them.
Smaller areas mean more detail but fewer published tables, more privacy noise, and larger margins of error. ACS 5-year estimates are the only ACS product for tracts and block groups.
An API lets your code request data from a server. A REST request is an endpoint URL plus parameters, and the response is usually JSON.
tidycensus wraps the Census API: get_acs() and get_decennial() return tidy data frames, and geometry = TRUE makes them map-ready.
Convert counts to shares with summary_var, carry margins of error through calculations with the moe_*() functions, and compare across years only with non-overlapping periods, consistent boundaries, and inflation-adjusted dollars.

6.9 Exercises

Reading GEOIDs. The GEOID 370630020271003 identifies a Census block. Which state, county, tract, and block group does it belong to? How many digits does each part have?
Choosing a source. For each question, name the survey (decennial, ACS 1-year, or ACS 5-year) and the smallest geography you could use. (a) How many housing units are in each block in Durham? (b) What was median household income in Wake County last year? (c) What share of residents in each Chapel Hill neighborhood rent their home?
Build a URL. Write by hand the Census API URL that requests total population (B01003_001E) for every county in Virginia (state FIPS 51) from the 2022 ACS 5-year data. Paste it into a browser to check it. Then reproduce the same request with httr2.
Reliability. Download median household income for every block group in Orange County, NC. What share of block groups have a CV above 30%? Repeat for tracts and compare.
A rate map. Map the share of households with no vehicle available for tracts in your home county, or in Mecklenburg County, NC. Use B25044 and include the margin of error of the share.
Change over time. Compare median gross rent (B25064_001) for North Carolina counties in the 2013–2017 and 2018–2022 ACS. Which counties saw the largest increase? Explain why you should adjust for inflation, and what else could make your comparison misleading.
Your own question. Return to the question you wrote down in Section 6.3. Download the data you need, make a map, and write one paragraph interpreting it, including what the margins of error tell you about your confidence.

6.10 Further reading

Kyle Walker, the author of tidycensus, has written a free online book, Analyzing US Census Data: Methods, Maps, and Models in R (Walker 2023). It covers everything in this chapter in more depth and is the best next step for any project that uses Census data.
The tidycensus documentation, at https://walker-data.com/tidycensus, has vignettes on spatial data, margins of error, and microdata.
The Census Bureau’s ACS handbooks explain how the survey works and how to handle margins of error (U.S. Census Bureau 2020).
To browse tables without code, use data.census.gov, then bring the variable codes you find back to load_variables() and tidycensus.

title: Glossary
text:
Key terms used in this book. In the chapters, a term with a dotted underline shows its definition when you hover over it, tap it, or reach it with the Tab key.


1-year estimates

ACS estimates from 12 months of responses. They are the most current but are only published for areas of 65,000 people or more.

5-year estimates

ACS estimates that pool 60 months of responses. They are the most reliable ACS product and the only one for tracts and block groups. An estimate labeled 2022 describes 2018 to 2022.

American Community Survey (ACS)

The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every value is an estimate with a margin of error.

ANOVA

Analysis of variance: a statistical test of whether the averages of several groups are different, such as average incomes in two cities.

API

Application Programming Interface: a set of rules for how one program asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the Census Bureau’s server for a table.

API key

A private code that identifies you to an API. Store it in .Renviron, never in a script you share.

apportionment

Dividing the seats in the House of Representatives among the states by population, the reason the Constitution requires a census.

argument

An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.

assignment operator

<-, the arrow that stores the value on its right in the name on its left. Read x <- 5 as “x gets 5.”

block group

A group of census blocks, usually holding 600 to 3,000 people. It is the smallest geography with ACS 5-year estimates.

block of code

Several lines of code that work together on one task, like the steps of one recipe. In R Markdown, a block usually lives in one code chunk.

Boolean

Another name for logical (TRUE or FALSE) values, after the mathematician George Boole.

camelCase

A way of naming variables that joins words and capitalizes every word after the first, as in popChapelHill.

case-sensitive

Treating capital and lowercase letters as different. In R, Months and months are two different names.

census block

The smallest Census geography, often a single city block bounded by streets or other visible features. Only decennial census data are published for blocks.

census tract

A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood analysis.

character

The data type for text, also called strings. Character values always go inside quotation marks, as in "Chapel Hill".

cheatsheet

A one-page summary of a package or tool. Posit publishes them for dplyr, ggplot2, RStudio, and more.

clustering

Methods that find groups of similar observations, or groups of places with similar values that sit close together.

code chunk

A block of R code inside an R Markdown file, starting with ```{r} and ending with three backticks.

coefficient of variation (CV)

The standard error as a percentage of the estimate. A CV above about 30% is a common sign that an estimate is unreliable.

coercion

R converting values from one data type to another. Mixing types in one vector coerces them all to the type that can hold everything, usually character.

colon operator

:, which makes a sequence of whole numbers: 6:8 is c(6, 7, 8).

comment

A note for people that R ignores. In R, a comment starts with #.

comparison operator

An operator that compares two values and returns TRUE or FALSE: >, <, >=, <=, == (equal to), and != (not equal to).

compiler

A program that translates a whole program into machine code before any of it runs. C and Java are compiled; R is interpreted.

confidence level

How sure you can be that the true value lies within a range. The ACS uses a 90% confidence level for its margins of error.

Console

The RStudio pane (bottom left) where R runs commands and prints results, warnings, and errors. Nothing typed here is saved.

coordinate system

The rules that tie coordinates to places on the Earth, including how the round Earth is flattened onto a map (the projection). Layers must share a coordinate system before you can combine them.

CRAN

The Comprehensive R Archive Network: the official website for downloading R and most R packages.

CSV

A plain-text table in which each line is a row and commas separate the values. Read one into R with read.csv() or read_csv().

data frame

R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.

data science workflow

The steps of a data analysis: import, tidy, then a loop of transform, visualize, and model, and finally communicate.

data type

The kind of value R is storing. The four main atomic types are logical, integer, numeric, and character; class() tells you which you have.

debugging

Finding and fixing the mistakes (bugs) in code: read the error message, find the line, make a guess, and test it.

decennial census

The full count of everyone in the US, every ten years. It asks only a few questions but covers every person.

delimiter

The character that separates values in a text file of data, such as a comma in a CSV file or a tab.

Demographic and Housing Characteristics (DHC)

The 2020 census product with more detailed tables on age, sex, households, and housing than the redistricting data.

denominator

The number you divide by to turn a count into a share, usually the total of the same table, such as total population.

differential privacy

Carefully calibrated random noise added to published 2020 census tables to protect respondents’ privacy. It matters most for small areas such as blocks.

dplyr

The tidyverse package for transforming data frames: filtering rows, choosing columns, adding new columns, joining tables, and summarizing.

Editor

The RStudio pane (top left) where you write and save scripts and R Markdown files. Code here can be kept and run again.

endpoint

The web address of one dataset or service in an API, such as https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5.

Environment

The RStudio pane (top right) that lists the variables and data currently in memory.

file path

The location of a file on your computer, such as data/counties.csv. When you knit, paths are read relative to the folder the .Rmd file is saved in.

FIPS code

A standard numeric code for a state or county (Federal Information Processing Standards). North Carolina is 37.

first law of geography

Waldo Tobler’s statement that “everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” It is the idea behind spatial autocorrelation.

function

Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output, such as mean(temps).

geocoding

Turning an address or place name into coordinates that can be mapped.

GEOID

The unique ID of a Census area, made by stringing together the FIPS codes of each level, such as 37135 for Orange County, NC. Keep GEOIDs as text, and join tables on them.

ggplot2

The tidyverse package for making plots and maps by adding layers.

header

The first line of a data file, when it holds the column names.

help page

A function’s documentation, opened with ?name or help(name). Every help page has a Description, Usage, Arguments, and Examples.

hotspot

A cluster of places with unusually high values, such as a group of neighborhoods with many burglaries. Finding hotspots is a common goal of spatial analysis.

HTTP

The protocol web browsers and servers use to talk. A GET request reads data; a POST request sends data.

httr2

An R package for building, sending, and reading web (HTTP) requests, used to call an API by hand.

independence

The assumption, built into most standard statistics, that knowing one observation tells you nothing about another. Data about places usually break it, because nearby places tend to be alike.

indexing

Selecting part of a vector or data frame with square brackets: by position (vect[3]), by a condition (vect[vect > 10]), or by name (vect["Fozzie"]).

integer

The data type for whole numbers. R stores a typed number as numeric unless you add an L, as in 21L. Shown as <int> by glimpse().

integrated development environment (IDE)

A program that puts everything for writing code in one window: an editor, a place to run the code, and tools to inspect the results.

interpreted language

A language, like R, that runs code one line at a time: an interpreter reads each line, translates it, and runs it before moving on.

Jenks natural breaks

A way of dividing values into map classes that puts the breaks where the gaps between values are largest, so similar values share a color.

join

Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with left_join().

JSON

JavaScript Object Notation: structured text that most web APIs send back, which R can turn into lists or data frames.

knit

To build an R Markdown file into a finished document (HTML, PDF, or Word). Knitting reruns every code chunk from the top in a fresh R session.

library

The folder on your computer where installed packages are stored. You install packages into a library, then load them with library().

logical

The data type for TRUE and FALSE values, written in capitals with no quotation marks.

logical operator

An operator that combines TRUE and FALSE values: & (AND, both must be true), | (OR, either can be true), and ! (NOT).

logical vector

A vector of TRUE and FALSE values, such as the result of vect > 10. Inside square brackets it keeps the TRUE positions.

margin of error (MOE)

How far a sample estimate might be from the true value. ACS margins of error use a 90% confidence level: there is a 90% chance the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the MOE.

Markdown

A simple way of formatting plain text: # for headings, *italic*, **bold**, and - for list items.

masking

When two loaded packages have a function with the same name, the one loaded later hides (masks) the other. Reach the hidden one with package::function().

mean center of population

The point where a flat map of the country would balance if every resident weighed the same.

median

The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.

metadata

Data about data: who made a dataset, when, how, and what each part means. In a YAML header, it describes the document.

microdata

Records for individual people or households (with identifying details removed), rather than totals for areas. The ACS publishes microdata as PUMS.

missing value

A value that is unknown, written NA (“not available”) in R. Most calculations with NA give NA; test for it with is.na().

modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)

The way results can change when the same individual data are grouped into different areas, either larger or smaller ones or the same size with different boundaries.

named argument

An argument given with its name, such as digits = 1 in round(x, digits = 1).

negative index

An index with a minus sign, such as vect[-3], which drops that position and returns the rest.

nesting

When every smaller area lies entirely inside exactly one larger area, as blocks do inside block groups, tracts, and counties. Nested areas can be added up without double-counting anyone.

network analysis

Analysis of movement along a network, such as roads, to measure travel distance or time, or how easily people can reach a place.

nominal dollars

Dollar amounts as reported in their own year, not adjusted for inflation. Adjust them before comparing across years.

numeric

The data type for numbers that can have a decimal part, such as 103.21. Also called double, and shown as <dbl> by glimpse().

nycflights13

An R package of data on every flight that left New York City’s three airports in 2013, including the flights data frame.

observation

One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.

package

A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R. Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in each session with library().

parameter

A name=value setting added to an API request after the ?, such as for=county:*, that says what you want.

pipe

The operator |>, which passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then.”

polygon

A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a census tract.

program

A set of lines and blocks of code that work together to do a whole job. R runs a program from top to bottom, so order matters.

purrr

The tidyverse package for repeating a task over many inputs, such as downloading data for several years.

Quarto

The newer successor to R Markdown, from the same developers. Quarto files end in .qmd. This book is written in Quarto.

R Markdown

A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished report.

R script

A plain file of R code, ending in .R. Anything that isn’t code must be written as a comment.

R session

One run of R, from start to finish. A new session starts with an empty Environment and no packages loaded; knitting always starts a fresh one.

raster

Spatial data stored as a grid of cells (pixels), each holding a value, such as a satellite image or an elevation model. In R, the terra package handles rasters.

recycling

R repeating a shorter vector until it matches the length of a longer one, so vect[c(TRUE, FALSE)] keeps every other element.

redistricting data (PL 94-171)

The first 2020 census product: basic population, race, voting-age, and housing counts down to the block, used to redraw voting districts.

regression

A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).

reproducibility

The ability for anyone to rerun an analysis from its code and data and get the same result.

REST

The most common style of web API: each dataset has its own URL, you ask for data with ordinary web requests, and the answer usually comes back as JSON.

RStudio

The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R. R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.

sample

A subset of a population that is surveyed to estimate something about the whole population. Smaller samples give less certain estimates.

scale

The level of detail at which you study something: addresses, neighborhoods, counties, or states. A pattern that is clear at one scale can vanish or reverse at another.

sf

“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line, or polygon.

snake_case

A way of naming variables with lowercase words joined by underscores, as in pop_chapel_hill. The tidyverse style guide uses it.

spatial autocorrelation

The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar incomes.

spatial data science

The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions (science).

spatial heterogeneity

The idea that relationships between variables change from place to place. A link that is strong in one city may be weak, or reversed, in another.

spatial thinking

Taking seriously how location connects observations: asking whether nearby values are alike, whether a pattern depends on the size of the areas, and whether a relationship holds everywhere.

standard error

A measure of how much a sample estimate would vary from sample to sample. For the ACS, it is the margin of error divided by 1.645.

syntax

The exact rules for writing code: spelling, capitalization, commas, quotation marks, and matching brackets.

terra

An R package for working with raster data.

tidy data

Data arranged so that each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value has its own cell.

tidycensus

An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and returns it as a tidy data frame, with boundaries attached if you ask.

tidyverse

A family of R packages (including dplyr, ggplot2, and readr) for reading, cleaning, reshaping, summarizing, and plotting data, all designed to work together.

TIGER

The Census Bureau’s national digital map database of streets and boundaries, first used for the 1990 census. Census boundary files come from it.

tigris

An R package that downloads Census boundary files (TIGER/Line shapefiles) as sf objects.

tmap

An R package for making thematic maps quickly, with sensible defaults.

truth table

A table listing the result of a logical operator for every combination of TRUE and FALSE inputs.

variable

In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic, such as median income; each Census variable has a code.

vector

A sequence of values that R stores together, made with c(), such as c(71, 75, 68).

vector data

Spatial data stored as points, lines, and polygons, each with a table of attributes. In R, the sf package handles vector data.

verb

A dplyr function named for the job it does to a data frame, such as filter(), select(), arrange(), and mutate().

wrapper package

An R package that hides the details of calling an API behind simple functions, such as tidycensus for the Census API.

YAML header

The block at the top of an R Markdown file, between two lines of three dashes, that holds the document’s title, author, date, and output format.

ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA)

The Census Bureau’s approximation of a ZIP code’s area, built from census blocks. ZCTAs do not nest inside counties or tracts.
